ch071.note: The source has shifeng, "to lose the wind" — thieves' and gamblers' cant for being caught out or having a job go wrong, as a ship loses the wind and founders.

Yang Jinkui and Han Caigou are named in the sketch as the two most celebrated pickpockets of the day; neither is recorded elsewhere, and the names have the ring of underworld nicknames (Han Caigou reads as "Han the Clever Dog").

ch072.note: Chi doufu, "to eat tofu" — Shanghai slang, then and now, for taking liberties with a woman, from a flirtatious remark to a grope. The phrase glossed just below it in the source, diao bangzi (rendered "to hook a woman by the arm"), is the plainer term for the same thing.

Baixiangren, from the Wu verb baixiang, "to play, to amuse oneself" — the Shanghai word for an idle man-about-town, its sense running from a harmless street-loafer to a petty gangster. It is rendered "hoodlum" throughout this book; one later sketch is titled "The Hoodlum's Missus" (baixiangren saosao).

Lu Zhonglian (also Lu Lian), a persuader of the Warring States period celebrated for talking rulers out of their crises and then refusing every reward and office offered him. To "set oneself up as a Lu Zhonglian" is to pose as a selfless helper.

Wu Zhihui (1865–1953), one of the four revered elders of the Kuomintang, a classical scholar and satirist who had been an anarchist during his years in France and who chaired the commission that standardized Mandarin pronunciation; in these years an elder statesman close to Chiang Kai-shek.

Rong Zongjing (1873–1938), known as the "Flour King," who with his younger brother Rong Desheng built the Maoxin and Fuxin flour mills and the Shenxin cotton-spinning combine, the largest Chinese-owned textile group of the Republic. In 1934 the Shenxin combine fell into the severe liquidity crisis the author calls his "cash-flow troubles," which dates this sketch to about that year. (Corroborated.)

Chen Gongbo (1892–1946), a leader of the Kuomintang's left wing who served as Minister of Industry from the end of 1931 to the end of 1935 — hence the natural addressee of an appeal on a manufacturer's behalf. He later became a principal of Wang Jingwei's collaborationist regime and was executed for treason in 1946. (Corroborated.)
Chi baishi, "to eat white" — to eat a free meal at another's expense, to sponge. The author derives the underworld's "eating tofu" from it by way of the pun on white.

ch072.anchor: making one's success off the backs of others
ch072.note: Wu Zhihui's sense turns on yin ren cheng shi, a set phrase (from the tale of Mao Sui in the Records of the Grand Historian) meaning "to get one's business done by relying on others" — here, the safe man who coasts on other people's effort and risk, which the author distinguishes from the loafer's "eating tofu."

ch073.note: Biaojin, "standard gold" — the standardized gold bars traded on the Shanghai Gold Exchange, quoted and settled by the bar (tiao).
Yangpan, Shanghai slang for a greenhorn or dupe, one there to be fleeced. The stronger form da yangpan, the "big silver sucker," punning on the silver dollar, appears in an earlier sketch.
Fan menkan, "to flip the threshold" — brokers' cant for taking a customer for a fool, which the author glosses in the text itself.
Qiang maozi and lao maozi, "snatching" and "scooping the hat" — brokers' cant for scalping: darting in and out of the market to skim a quick turn off a small move in the price.

Chi panzi, the racket that gives the sketch its title: the broker buys the client's gold in at the true market price but reports a higher one, so that on top of his fixed commission he keeps the whole difference.

ch074.note: Hongbai shi, "red and white affairs": weddings, whose color is the red of joy, and funerals, whose color is the white of mourning. The author supplies the gloss himself.
Erye, "second masters" — male attendants hired by the day to help run a household's weddings and funerals.
Xiniang, the matron engaged to dress and attend the bride and to guide her through the wedding rites.

Chi baijia fan, "to eat from a hundred households" — to live off casual work at many different families' celebrations; the phrase carries the sense of a scattered, precarious, hand-to-mouth living, which is why the author can stretch it to "a thousand households, ten thousand."
Qingke chuan, genteel amateurs who play music or perform opera at other people's celebrations — not paid, but feasted.

Jituan jiehun, the collective civil wedding ceremonies promoted under the New Life Movement as a plain and thrifty alternative to the lavish old rites. Shanghai's municipal government held the first in April 1935 under Mayor Wu Tiecheng, which places this sketch in 1935 or after. (Corroborated.)

ch075.note: Jiaohun, "calling back the soul," also softened to jiaoxi, "calling back the joy": the folk remedy for a child (or an adult) thought to have been startled out of its soul, whose loss is blamed for sleeplessness or sickness. The rite is worked by two people calling and answering antiphonally, the caller's ju (a dialect word the author glosses as "return") coaxing the wandering soul home.
A-nan, a Wu-dialect endearment for a small child (the nan written with the character for a girl-child); here it stands in for the sick child's own pet name.
Anxixiang, benzoin or storax resin, burned as incense; its Chinese name reads literally "peace-and-rest incense," which suits a rite meant to settle a troubled soul.

Jiama, woodblock-printed paper offerings burned to summon or send off spirits. The count of forty-nine — seven sevens — is the same ritually potent number that governs the seven weeks of Chinese mourning.
The returning soul is believed to alight in the small spider that turns up at the end of the search; caught and carried home under the pillow, the spider is the soul brought back.

ch076.note: Mayi zhai, "mourning-cloth debt": money lent to a spendthrift heir against his expectations, on a note that falls due only when his tight-fisted father dies and the son puts on the coarse hemp (mayi) of a mourner. The morbidity is the point — the loan is a bet on the old man's death.

Yinzi qian (here written yinzi dian), "stamp-money": a form of installment usury in which the lender stamps his seal (yinzi) in the borrower's little book at each repayment, so called for the chop that marks off the shrinking debt.
Piqiu, "rubber ball" — usurers' cant for another kind of short loan, listed here beside the others; the sense of the name is not certain and it is left literal.
Yijiao guoye, "a jiao overnight" — a petty overnight loan lent at ruinous interest. A jiao is a tenth of a dollar (see the note on money at the New Year sketch).
Shen zhi le jiao, "straightened out his legs" — a blunt colloquial euphemism for dying; the author plays on it again at the close with the fathers whose "two legs are yet unstraightened."

ch077.note: Xinglong piao, "prosperity note": the promissory note a bankrupt shopkeeper hands his creditors, promising to repay "once business is thriving again" — with no date and no interest, it is a polite fiction by which everyone agrees to close the books on a debt that will never be paid. Xinglong is the "flourishing, thriving" a shop-sign wishes on a business.

ch077.anchor: shut up shop and be done
ch077.note: Guanmen daji, literally "close the door — great good luck," the stock ironic phrase for going out of business.
The source enumerates the creditors jia, yi, bing, ding, the first four of the ten Heavenly Stems, used exactly as English uses A, B, C, D for unnamed parties.

ch078.note: A yang ge, "Brother Sheep": the pleasure quarter's name for a rich, ugly, loutish patron worth flattering only for his money — a sheep (yang) to be fleeced, the word punning on the yang of yangpan, the sucker of the sketch's first line.
The source has maike maike, a reduplicated bit of Shanghai pidgin from the English "much much" — meaning the man is rolling in money.
Qusi, "wronged to death": another cant term for the greenhorn who is bled dry and can only swallow it, here fastened onto the know-nothing who struts as a man of the world.

ch079.note: Shuigui, "water ghost" — here not a spirit but a professional diver, hired to go down after drowned bodies and sunken cargo when a ship is wrecked.

Wusong, the anchorage where the Huangpu empties into the Yangtze at the northern edge of Shanghai, and Hongkou, the district just north of Suzhou Creek — both on the water, and both then thick with dockside and riverfront trades.

ch079.anchor: protective suit of supple leather that passes the air
ch079.note: Baoxian yi, a "safety garment": the author is describing the period diving-dress. His phrase that the leather "passes the air" (touqi) reflects that such a suit was fed air from the surface; a diver not bred to the water, he adds, would drown in it regardless.

ch080.note: Mai yang, "selling sheep": Shanghai abuse for a two-faced impostor, one who is not what he shows himself to be. As the author explains, it is a clipped form of the next idiom.

ch080.anchor: hang up a sheep's head and sell dog's flesh
ch080.note: Gua yang tou, mai gou rou, "to hang up a sheep's head but sell dog's flesh" — the classic phrase for passing off one thing under the sign of another, for fraud and false pretenses.
Chi gongshi fan, "to eat official rice": to be on the government's payroll. The baotan named here is a plainclothes police detective, the jicha an inspector.

ch081.note: Maixiang, "salable looks" — a good, presentable appearance, the quality of "selling well" by how one looks. The word is still in everyday use, now most often for the eye-appeal of goods on a stall.

ch081.anchor: talking ghost-talk to a ghost and man-talk to a man
ch081.note: Jian gui shuo gui hua, jian ren shuo ren hua — the stock phrase for the glib chameleon who tailors his words to whoever stands before him.

ch081.anchor: judging a man by his looks, and so being wrong about Ziyu
ch081.note: Yi mao qu ren, shi zhi Ziyu — Confucius's rueful admission, recorded in the Records of the Grand Historian, that he had once misjudged his disciple Tantai Ziyu, whose homely face belied a worthy man. The Master's paired confession was that he had also erred by trusting the fine talk of Zai Yu.

ch081.anchor: a pen that could dash off a thousand words leaning against a horse
ch081.note: Yi ma qian yan, "a thousand words leaning on a horse" — from the tale of Yuan Hong, who, ordered to draft a proclamation, leaned against his horse and reeled off sheet after sheet without pause; the byword for swift, copious composition.
Qianke, a broker or commission middleman — literally a "shoulder-carrier," one who carries a deal between buyer and seller for his cut.

ch082.note: The author reaches for the fashionable translated vocabulary of the day: youxian jieji, "the leisure class," and kuaile zhuyi, literally "pleasure-ism," hedonism — the new sociologist's words dropped, half in fun, onto a page about caged birds.
Xiaokai, the "young boss": the son and heir of a shopkeeping family, living at ease on the business, which the author glosses in the text.
Chong niao, "flushing the birds": carrying one's caged songbirds out at daybreak to air them and let them sing in the open, and then, as the sketch says, to sit over tea with the other fanciers.

Liu malu, the sixth of the numbered east-west roads of the Settlement (after Nanjing, Jiujiang, Hankou, Fuzhou and Guangdong Roads); this is Beihai Road, laid out in 1883 along the curve of the old racecourse.

The Longyuan ("Dragon Garden") teahouse; the Leyi and Shangle named just after it stood in the City God Temple bazaar in the old walled city. All three were haunts where the bird-fanciers gathered after the morning airing.

ch083.anchor: turning the luck with a wedding
ch083.note: Chongxi, "to charge away [ill fortune] with joy": the custom of hurrying a betrothed bride into the house of a gravely ill relative, in the belief that the joy of a wedding will drive off the sickness — here for a sick parent, though it was as often worked for a dying son.

ch083.anchor: sink past cure into the vitals
ch083.note: Bing ru gaohuang, "the sickness has entered the gao and the huang" — the fat below the heart and the membrane above the diaphragm, where (in the Zuo Commentary's tale of the Marquis of Jin) no needle or medicine can reach. The byword for an illness past all cure.

ch083.anchor: two provinces of Jiangsu and Zhejiang
ch083.note: Jiangsu and Zhejiang, the two wealthy provinces of the Yangtze delta that flank Shanghai and supplied most of its migrants.

ch084.note: Zhaohui: the word means a diplomatic note, but here it is a vehicle permit. Because Shanghai was split among separate jurisdictions, a rickshaw needed a different license nailed up for each zone it was allowed to ply.

ch084.anchor: the Chinese city, the British Settlement, and the French Concession
ch084.note: The three Shanghais: the Chinese-governed municipality (huajie), the International Settlement (here called the "British" Settlement, after its founders), and the French Concession. A rickshaw plying all three carried a plate for each.
The author notes that da, "big," is pronounced du in this phrase — a Wu-dialect reading of the character.

ch085.note: Huangbaoche, the "yellow-hood cart": the man-pulled two-wheeled rickshaw that was the common conveyance of the city.

ch085.anchor: a gold quarter-piece as though it were silver dimes
ch085.note: The source has jin si kai, a "gold quarter-piece" — a small gold coin worth a quarter (perhaps a quarter-sovereign); the sense is that the foreigner throws his gold about as a Chinese would his small silver. The yang dian just before it is foreign silver, spent, the puller imagines, as freely as coppers.
Qiuba, a slighting slang word for a common soldier — the characters 丘 and 八 stacked together spell 兵, "soldier." Here they are foreign servicemen on a spree.

ch085.anchor: an imported ham and five foreign cigars
ch085.note: The sting is in the slang: a kick, in Shanghai talk, was a "ham" (huotui), and by the same wit the "five cigars" are the five fingers of a slap. The puller who hoped for a gold sovereign comes away instead with a foreign boot and a foreign clout.

ch086.note: The sketch turns on piaoliang, which means at once "good-looking, classy" and "handsome, open-handed." A piaoliang renwu is a man who wants to cut the figure of the grand, free-spending gentleman — and the puller's jibe below, that this is a "duck-piss-stinking" sort of piaoliang, plays on the man who wants the style without paying for it.

Jiangbei (Subei), the poorer country north of the Yangtze, supplied the great majority of Shanghai's rickshaw-pullers, who were a standing butt of local contempt; the "worthy elder brother" (renxiong) is said with a sneer.

ch087.note: Xiaoche, the "small cart": the single-wheeled push-cart, worked by a man shoving from behind, which carried both freight and (perched on the frame to either side of the wheel) passengers.
Goutou che, "dog's-head cart," a nickname for the wheelbarrow.

ch087.anchor: the early years of the Tongzhi reign
ch087.note: The Tongzhi reign ran 1862–1874; the author dates the wheelbarrow's Shanghai debut to its first years.

ch087.anchor: the end of the Guangxu and the beginning of the Xuantong reigns
ch087.note: That is, about 1908–1911, the last years of the Qing, when the motorcar and the electric tram reached the city.
Dongyang che, the "Eastern-Ocean cart" — the rickshaw, so called because it came by way of Japan.
Zhabei, the Chinese industrial district north of the Settlement, thick with factories and the workers who staffed them.

ch088.note: Da chusang, the "grand funeral": the vast, costly funeral procession of a rich or famous man, which the author glosses as the jubin, the funeral cortege. Such processions were among the great free spectacles of the city, drawing crowds from far outside it.

Sheng Xuanhuai (1844–1916), by his courtesy name Xingsun: the late-Qing official and industrialist often called the father of Chinese industry, founder of the China Merchants Steam Navigation Company, the imperial telegraph, and China's first modern bank and university. His funeral procession wound through Shanghai on 18 November 1917, reportedly more than a mile long and watched by something approaching a million people; it was filmed as what is said to be China's first newsreel. (Corroborated.)

Zhu Baosan (1848–1926), a Ningbo man who rose from a hardware apprentice to be a British firm's comprador and one of Shanghai's greatest merchants, three times president of the Chinese General Chamber of Commerce. The French Concession honored him in his own lifetime with a street bearing his name, the Rue Chu Pao San (pictured); his death in 1926 brought another of the city's famous grand funerals. (Corroborated.)

Huang Chujiu, the amusement-hall and patent-medicine magnate met in earlier sketches (builder of the Great World), died in January 1931 — "the year before last," which places this piece about 1933. He died so deep in debt that the grand funeral the crowds expected of him was quietly dropped. (Corroborated.)

ch088.anchor: an inborn bad streak in the Chinese character
ch088.note: Liegenxing, a "bad root-nature": the fashionable idea of the day, sharpened by Lu Xun and the May Fourth writers, that the Chinese people carried some ingrained national failing. The author enlists it against the mob's craving for spectacle.

ch088.anchor: a bridge collapses at a temple festival
ch088.note: The temple-festival parades (saihui) drew such crushes that fatal stampedes and the collapse of overloaded bridges were real and recurring disasters — the calamity the author says the crowd "gawks up" for itself.

ch089.note: Songsang mache, the "funeral carriage": the horse-drawn carriage, once the smartest way to ride, reduced by the coming of the motorcar to carrying mourners — the name, the author says, could not fit its fallen estate better.

ch089.anchor: reorganized into the Yunfei Motor Company
ch089.note: The Longfei ("Dragon-Flight") carriage firm by the Racecourse gave way to the Yunfei ("Cloud-Flight") Motor Company, one of the largest and best-remembered of early Shanghai's taxi firms, its fleet turned out in a single livery. (Corroborated.)

Yugong: men of means living in retirement or self-imposed exile far from their native places — ex-officials, retired merchants, and the like, of whom the safety of the concessions drew a great many to Shanghai.
Yaozi hong guniang: the yaozi was a low brothel, and its hong guniang, "red girls," were its popular, sought-after ones.

ch090.note: Beng changmian, to "hold the show taut" — to keep up a front, to save face by display; the whole theme of the sketch.

ch090.anchor: Silk draped down the back, and no rice for supper at home
ch090.note: A Shanghai proverb (shen shang chou pipi, jia li meiyou yefan mi): fine silk on one's back and not a grain of rice for the evening meal — all show and no substance.
Zhong shi zeng hua, "to tread in the footsteps and add flourishes" — a literary phrase for taking what others have done and making it grander still.
The source has zhaitai gao zhu, "to build the debt-terrace high" — the idiom comes from King Nan of Zhou, who is said to have fled his creditors to a high terrace; it means to be buried under debt.
Tangguan, the waiter of a restaurant or teahouse, whose good opinion the show is partly meant to buy.

ch091.note: The doses are given in apothecary weights: a tael (liang) is about 37 grams, and a mace (qian) a tenth of that. The point is that ginseng is potent stuff, to be taken by the measured dose.

ch091.anchor: grown in the province of Jilin
ch091.note: Wild ginseng from the forests of Jilin, in Manchuria, and from Korea was the costliest grade; the cheap ‘garden ginseng’ of the next paragraph is the cultivated root, which the trade doctored and passed off as wild.
Yingkou, a treaty port in southern Manchuria, where the season’s ginseng was brought down to market.
A picul (dan) is a carrying-pole load of a hundred catties (jin), roughly sixty kilograms — here fetching only two or three dollars in bulk, against the hundreds a doctored root would bring.

ch092.note: Xutou, the ‘empty’ or padded margin in an asking price. The haggling that follows was proverbial: the seller ‘asks the sky’ (xiang tian tao jia), pitching his price absurdly high, and the buyer must ‘offer the ground’ (zhuo di huan dian), bidding absurdly low, so that the two may meet somewhere in the middle.

ch093.anchor: spoken of here is not the lowest grade
ch093.note: Yeji, ‘wild chicken’ or pheasant, is the Shanghai word for the lowest, unlicensed streetwalker (see chapter 12). Here the author shows how the tag spread to anything freelance, unlicensed or off the books: the ‘pheasant’ carriage the driver owns and works on his own account, the ‘pheasant’ broker outside the guild, and the ‘beating the pheasant’ of the theater ticket-tout below.

ch094.note: Ransom-kidnapping (bangpiao) grew into an organized racket in and around Shanghai in the 1920s and 1930s, striking especially at men known to have money — which is why a propertied doctor, called out to a stranger, feared for himself.

ch094.anchor: a guarantee be signed and stamped
ch094.note: The baodan, a bond of surety: a note by which some established shop, vouched for by its seal, stood warrant that the caller was genuine and the doctor would come to no harm.

ch095.note: ‘Pheasant’ here carries the extended slang sense set out in chapters 12 and 93 — not the bird but the cheap, unlicensed, off-the-books article: roadside rice-dumplings of no fixed maker.

ch096.note: The old copper reckoning: a hundred cash (wen) made ten of the larger copper coins (tongyuan). Against this the squat pole’s bowl at a mao in small silver was the dearer fare.

ch097.note: The kefan or set meal: a flat charge for two dishes, a soup and all the rice one could eat — the cheapest square meal in the city, and the ancestor of the modern ‘combination’ plate.

ch097.anchor: Muslim eating-houses outside the Old North Gate
ch097.note: The jiaomenguan, restaurants kept by Hui (Chinese Muslim) proprietors, which the author credits with inventing the set meal. The Old North Gate was a gate of Shanghai’s old walled city, and the streets outside it a run of cheap eating-houses.

ch098.note: Kaiyou, ‘wiping off the oil’ — skimming a private cut off the customer’s cloth. The word recurs throughout the book and gives the title of chapter 152; here it is the tailor’s standing perquisite, filched a pinch at a time from every length of stuff.

ch098.anchor: The tailor who does not filch his cloth
ch098.note: The proverb turns on the Wu word for a wife, jiazhupo, literally the ‘mistress of the house’: a tailor so honest as never to filch would starve, and end by pawning his own wife.

ch099.anchor: laid out for sale on stalls
ch099.note: Lengtan, the ‘cold stalls’ — secondhand-book pitches, so named because the goods lay out cold and unminded until a buyer chanced by. Those in the City God Temple bazaar (see chapter 1) were the most famous.
Beitie: ink rubbings taken from engraved stone tablets, prized as models of calligraphy and collected like prints.

ch100.anchor: Xu Shaoqing ran the Dangui First Stage
ch100.note: The Dangui First Stage, founded on Fuzhou Road in 1867, was one of Shanghai’s oldest and grandest Peking-opera houses; Xu Shaoqing managed it until 1914. The account is corroborated by the theater’s history.

In the north, at Beiping (Beijing) and Tianjin, opera was something to be heard — the connoisseur closed his eyes for the singing; in Shanghai it was something to be watched, for the spectacle, so a distant box high up was no bargain however cheap.

ch101.note: The shop-names are those of famous confectioners: Daoxiangcun and Yebiqi of the older day, Lao Dafang and Tianlu of the new. Lao Dafang, a Suzhou-style house founded in 1842, was so imitated that by the 1930s some forty shops all traded under the name, each marked off only by an added character — exactly the ‘mark added above to tell one from another’ the author notes.

Xunyu, ‘smoked fish,’ is in fact not smoked but marinated in a sweet-spiced sauce and deep-fried, a standard cold relish; sutang, ‘crisp candy,’ is a brittle bar of sugar with ground sesame or peanut.

ch101.anchor: the addicts of Shanghai are many
ch101.note: Opium smokers: reclining at the lamp, the smoker liked a sweet to cut the bitterness of the drug (compare chapter 33), and the crisp-candy trade throve on the habit.

ch102.anchor: two hundred and eighty cash of standard coin
ch102.note: Zhiqian, the officially cast copper cash (wen) of the old currency. The author is measuring the inflation of half a century: a sum that once housed and fed a man for a day would not, by the 1930s, cover a servant’s tip.
The kezhan or guest-lodge, the old-fashioned Chinese inn, as against the Western-style hotel of the author’s own day.
The chafang, the inn or hotel manservant, who lived largely on his tips (xiaozhang).

ch103.anchor: the Land Regulations of the Settlement north of the Yangjingbang
ch103.note: The Yangjingbang was the creek that divided the International Settlement to its north from the French Concession to its south (it was filled in in 1915 to make Avenue Edward VII). The ‘Land Regulations north of the Yangjingbang’ were thus the by-laws of the International Settlement, enforced by its own police.

The source has the Wu vulgarism chai yang lanwu, ‘to loose a watery mess’ — here, to relieve oneself in the open. The idiom (also ‘chai lanwu’) more broadly means to make a slovenly, irresponsible mess of a thing.

ch104.note: Yanduidian, small shops that dealt at once in tobacco or opium and in the changing of money and small coin — much silver passing over the counter, hence the iron grille.

ch105.anchor: charity sharks is all they are
ch105.note: Shangun: the author’s coinage sets shan, ‘good’ or ‘charitable,’ against gun, a rascal or sharper — the man who works the machinery of good works for private gain. His closing pun on yigun, ‘righteousness sharks,’ turns the same trick on the relief funds for the Volunteer Army.
Maike maike, a bit of Shanghai pidgin from the English ‘much, much’ — money, and plenty of it (see chapter 78).

ch105.anchor: the funds subscribed for the Northeast Volunteer Army
ch105.note: The Northeast Volunteer Armies were the irregular anti-Japanese forces raised in Manchuria after its seizure in September 1931; Shanghai gave large sums for their relief in 1932, and public disputes over the handling of the money followed. The reference dates this essay to about 1933. The general facts are corroborated; the particulars of the scandal, as the author reports them, are not independently confirmed here.

ch106.anchor: a few score of society's notables
ch106.note: The advertising doctor bought respectability by getting well-known men to append their names to his notice in recommendation — a paid endorsement in all but name, and a staple of the patent-medicine and quack-doctor advertising that filled the Shanghai press.

ch107.note: ‘Superior Chinese’ (gaodeng huaren) was a jibe at the Chinese whom the foreign resident ranked above the common run — the compradors and well-placed sojourners who lived by foreign favor. The whole piece is a satire on that class, sharpened, as its close shows, by the author’s dread of a coming national ruin.

The maiban or comprador, the Chinese manager who ran a foreign firm’s business with the local market (compare Zhu Baosan, chapter 88); as a class the compradors grew rich and powerful in the treaty ports as the foreigner’s indispensable middlemen.

ch107.anchor: lick the boil and suck the piles
ch107.note: Shun yong shi zhi, ‘to lick the boil and suck the piles’ — a phrase from the Zhuangzi for the most abject and disgusting flattery, by which a toady wins his master’s favor.

ch107.anchor: the slaves of a conquered land
ch107.note: Wangguo nu, the ‘slaves of a fallen state.’ Written under the shadow of Japanese aggression in the early 1930s, the line warns the fawning ‘superior Chinese’ that foreign favor will not save them if the nation itself goes down.

ch108.note: Guilian, a ‘ghost-face’ — the sour, forbidding look a surly clerk turns on a customer he thinks beneath his trouble.
The author refers to an earlier piece of his own, ‘The Shop Clerk’s Three Faces’ — not one of the sketches in this volume.

ch109.anchor: a clock or a watch that has struck past its proper measure
ch109.note: This unpacks the slang shisandian, ‘thirteen o’clock’: a clock can strike no more than twelve, so one that strikes thirteen has gone one beyond its bound — the very image of a person not quite right in the head, a scatterbrain or half-wit.

The source calls her a mingling daughter. Mingling, a small caterpillar which an old belief held that the solitary wasp carried off and reared as its own, became in the Book of Songs the standing figure for an adopted child.

ch109.anchor: call him a dullard and he is no dullard
ch109.note: The 2019 reset prints an unusual character here for the ‘dullard’ word; it is read for plain sense, the phrase turning on a person who is neither quite a fool nor quite sharp.

ch110.note: Guaizi, child-stealers, who abducted children and bond-servant girls (bi) to be sold on — a traffic distinct from the ransom-kidnapping of chapter 94.

A common superstition: on a missing-person notice the character ren, ‘person,’ was printed upside-down, in the belief that so reversed it would keep the lost one from wandering far and bring him the sooner to hand.

ch111.anchor: the ballad-tales set to string and voice
ch111.note: Suzhou storytelling divides into dashu, the “big books” told in speech alone (military and heroic romances), and xiaoshu, the “little books”—tanci ballad-romances of love and domestic life, chanted to the three-stringed sanxian and the pipa. Only the sung little books open with a prelude. (Corroborated.)

ch111.anchor: he must always open with a prelude-song
ch111.note: The kaipian: a short, self-contained sung piece performed before the main story, both a warm-up and a display of vocal art. The tale proper follows, alternating spoken and sung passages. (Corroborated.)

Yu Xiushan, a tanci master of the early nineteenth century, whose refined, ornamented melody became the “Yu tune”—one of the three foundational schools of Suzhou tanci singing, alongside Chen Yugan’s “Chen tune” and Ma Rufei’s “Ma tune.” (Corroborated.)

Ma Rufei, a tanci master of the mid nineteenth century celebrated for The Pearl Pagoda. His plain, forthright “Ma tune” became the most widely imitated of all the tanci melodies and the root of many later schools. (Corroborated.)

ch112.anchor: The men who live off official business
ch112.note: Chi gongshi fan de, literally “those who eat the rice of official affairs”—the yamen clerks, runners and police whose living came from handling cases.
San xiatou, the “three intimidations”: a stock phrase for browbeating a suspect—or here a patient—into submission by frightening him.

ch112.anchor: at the foot of the pulse-record he never fails to write
ch112.note: The mai’an was the written record a Chinese physician kept of a patient’s pulse-signs, diagnosis and prescription. At its close a doctor conventionally added a formula of professional modesty, hou zheng (“awaiting your correction”), deferring his judgment to a more skilful colleague—here turned into a pre-emptive disclaimer of liability.

The text has gaohuang, the region between the heart and the diaphragm which classical medicine held beyond the reach of any remedy; a disease that has “entered the gaohuang” is proverbially incurable.

ch113.anchor: the provinces of Jin (Shanxi) and Sui (Suiyuan)
ch113.note: Two northern provinces given by their one-character literary names: Jin for Shanxi, Sui for Suiyuan (a province carved out of Inner Mongolia in 1928 and abolished in 1954, its territory now within the Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region).
Baimian, “white flour,” was the common street name for powdered heroin or morphine; the region named was a notorious transit ground for the northern drug trade. (Corroborated as a period term.)

ch113.anchor: this game of firing the big gun has turned up in Shanghai
ch113.note: Kai dapao, drug-users’ slang for smoking morphine packed into a hollowed-out cigarette. It has nothing to do with the same words’ ordinary meaning, “to talk big.”
Da danzi, “shooting marbles,” was slang for swallowing the cheap compounded narcotic pills—heroin or morphine cut with fillers—sold in the drug dens.

ch114.anchor: the eleventh year of the Republic
ch114.note: The renxu year is 1922, but the case is misdated. Yan Ruisheng murdered Wang Lianying in June 1920 (the ninth year of the Republic, the gengshen year) and was executed on 23 November 1920; the reprint advertisement reproduced with this sketch is itself dated 2 July 1920. Rendered as printed; the error is the author’s. (Contradicted by the record.)

Yan Ruisheng (1895–1920), a native of Tangyin in Henan and a former student of Aurora University, was an educated employee of a foreign firm ruined by gambling. Coveting the courtesan Wang Lianying’s diamond ring and jewels, he lured her by motor-car to a field outside the city and strangled her with accomplices, robbing her of ornaments worth some three thousand dollars; her body was found near Xujiahui. The sensational case became the subject of China’s first feature-length film and of stage plays for years after. (Corroborated.)
Fuxiang Li, the lane where Wang Lianying kept her rooms; li denotes one of the walled lane-neighbourhoods of old Shanghai.

The Songhu hujun shi, the senior military office over the Shanghai–Woosung district under the warlord governments; its holder was the highest authority the Chinese side could bring to bear on the case.
He Fenglin (1873–1935), courtesy name Maoru, a general of the Anhui clique who held the office of Songhu Defence Commissioner from 1920 to 1924. (Corroborated.)

ch114.anchor: son of the late Ningbo gentleman Zhu Baosan
ch114.note: Zhu Baosan (1848–1926), a Ningbo-born comprador and banker, was among the most powerful merchant-notables of Shanghai. That his son should be among the accused, and alone acquitted, is a detail the author lets stand without comment.

The New Stage (Xin Wutai), opened in 1908 at Jiumudi (“Nine-Mou Ground”) in the old Chinese city, was the first Western-style proscenium theatre run by Chinese and a cradle of reform drama. (Corroborated.)

Zhao Junyu, a popular stage actor known for female roles, and Wang Youyou (1888–1937), a pioneer of Chinese spoken drama (wenmingxi) and later film actor. The topical play capitalized on the case within weeks.

ch114.anchor: no less than that of Twin Sisters
ch114.note: Zimeihua (1934), Zheng Zhengqiu’s hugely popular sound film for the Mingxing company, with Hu Die in a double role. Its screening “this spring” places this sketch in 1934. (Corroborated.)

ch114.anchor: Later a ×× film company made it
ch114.note: The reprint blanks the company’s name. The 1921 feature Yan Ruisheng—often called China’s first full-length story film—was in fact made by the Chinese Cinema Study Society. (The suppressed name is not recoverable from the text.)

ch114.anchor: the Premier of the Flower Kingdom
ch114.note: Huaguo zongli. In the mock-republican “flower-kingdom elections” (see the note on the flower-election earlier in the book) the winning courtesans were awarded titles—President, Vice-President, Premier and the like. Wang Lianying took the Premier’s title at the New World’s election of 1917 (the dingsi year). (Corroborated.)

ch114.anchor: a student who left Aurora University
ch114.note: Zhendan Daxue, the French Jesuit university in Shanghai, founded in 1903. Yan Ruisheng had indeed studied there and was noted for his foreign languages. (Corroborated.)
Chaibai dang, the “peeling-white gang”—Shanghai’s confidence-men, who fleeced their victims through seduction, sham romance and blackmail; the word is here stretched to cover a robbery-murder.

ch115.note: A film-trade worker of this name; not identified in the standard film histories. (Uncorroborated.)

ch115.anchor: Mr. Yan Duhe, a reporter for the Xinwenbao
ch115.note: Yan Duhe (1889–1968), a leading Shanghai journalist who for more than thirty years edited the Xinwenbao’s celebrated literary supplement, the Kuaihuo Lin (“Happy Grove”); it was he who serialized Zhang Henshui’s Fate in Tears and Laughter. (Corroborated.)

ch115.anchor: issued an order forbidding women to perm their hair
ch115.note: The New Life Movement (Xin shenghuo yundong), launched by Chiang Kai-shek in February 1934 to reform public habits along frugal, disciplined, quasi-Confucian lines, campaigned against “decadent” fashions, permed hair among them. See also the note on the group weddings it promoted. (Corroborated.)

ch116.anchor: nearly every large shop has them fitted
ch116.note: Nianhongdeng, “year-red lamp,” was a period Shanghai name for the neon sign, more usually written nihongdeng (from ni-hong, “rainbow”). Neon advertising signs reached Shanghai in the 1920s and spread fastest along Nanjing Road. (Corroborated.)

ch116.anchor: The scientific name of the thing is
ch116.note: The author’s “scientific name,” nai guang, is from nai, the element neon; the reddish glow of the earliest commercial signs came from neon gas sealed in the tube. (Corroborated.)

ch117.note: Guihua, the sweet osmanthus (Osmanthus fragrans), a small autumn-flowering tree prized for its intense scent. Why Shanghai slang made its name a byword for the shoddy the author cannot explain.

ch117.anchor: why Guangxi is called the Cassia Province
ch117.note: The character gui serves both for the osmanthus and for the cassia-cinnamon tree, and is the one-character name of Guangxi province—hence “Cassia Province.” In what follows the author runs the two plants together, listing cassia (rougui, the source of cinnamon bark) among the “osmanthus.” (The conflation is his.)

ch117.anchor: is to signify a no-good woman and a bottom-grade lawyer
ch117.note: The Shanghai tags are guihua gualao and guihua lushi—contemptuous names for a worthless woman and a bottom-grade (unlicensed or incompetent) lawyer. The exact force of gualao is uncertain.

ch118.note: Huili qiu, jai alai or pelota, played for heavy betting at the Auditorium (the Hai-Alai court) on Avenue du Roi Albert in the French Concession.

ch118.anchor: his Complete Book of Getting Rich
ch118.note: Zhifu quanshu, a betting-guide purporting to teach systems for picking the winning huahui lottery numbers; see the note on the huahui earlier in the book.

ch118.anchor: the special scrip used inside the dog-track
ch118.note: Betting inside the tracks was done not in cash but in the house’s own chits, bought with silver at the gate—a device that kept the punters’ money inside the enclosure.

ch118.anchor: There used to be as many as three dog-tracks
ch118.note: The three greyhound tracks all opened about 1928: the Mingyuan (the Stadium) on Ward Road and the Shenyuan, both in the International Settlement, and the Yiyuan—the Canidrome—on Avenue du Roi Albert in the French Concession, built by the French entrepreneur J. J. Chollot and reckoned the largest gambling house in the Far East. Under pressure from Chinese opinion and the Nationalist government the two Settlement tracks were closed about 1931, leaving the Canidrome alone; the author’s account tallies with the record. (Corroborated.)

ch118.anchor: an electric hare runs out in front
ch118.note: The mechanical lure the dogs chase; the phrase renders dian tu, “electric rabbit.”

ch119.anchor: taking the sense from the shape
ch119.note: The pun is pictographic and doubly barbed. Read as numerals, one-two-three (yao-er-san) trace the sinuous line of the fashionable silhouette—bust thrust up, hips thrust back, the body swaying on high heels; and yao-er is at the same time the name of a middling grade of brothel (glossed earlier), so the tag hints that the modern girl is dressed like a courtesan.

ch120.anchor: an all-year itching in the clefts between the toes
ch120.note: The “damp” (shiqi) of Chinese medicine here means, in plain terms, the fungal infection of athlete’s foot, endemic in Shanghai’s humid climate; the festering the author goes on to describe is its worse form.

ch120.anchor: scrape the place once over with a little knife
ch120.note: The bathhouse kept a specialist, the paijiao jiang, who pared away the softened dead skin and calluses with a small blade—an early pedicurist.

ch121.note: Shuimenting, a Shanghai transliteration of the English “cement,” here the concrete pavement.
Chaizi, fortune-telling by taking a written character apart into its component strokes and radicals and reading omens from them.
The source has xiexing wenzi, “crab-crawling script,” a period Chinese nickname for the sideways-running writing of the Western alphabets.
Gaozhuang means literally “to lodge a complaint at law”; the beggars’ chalked appeals ape the form of a legal petition—hence the sketch’s title, “Petitions on the Pavement.”

ch122.anchor: the Pentang Lane Bridge, the Queen-of-Heaven Temple Bridge
ch122.note: Four crossings of Suzhou Creek. The Pentang Lane and Queen-of-Heaven Temple bridges are noted earlier in the book; the Old Lock Bridge (Laozha qiao) took its name from the old stone sluice-lock on the creek, and the “Rubbish Bridge” (Laji qiao) was a popular nickname earned from a refuse wharf beside it. On the steep bridge-approaches a loaded rickshaw slowed, and the beggars found their opening.

ch123.note: Biesan (written 瘛三), the classic Shanghai word for a penniless vagrant or guttersnipe. Its origin is disputed; one common guess derives it, by way of pidgin, from “empty” plus “cents.” (Corroborated as the term; the etymology is not.)
Renders dingshao qi qian, one of the recognized begging methods; dingshao, to shadow or tail a mark, is Wu-dialect cant and the exact image is uncertain.
Yangjingbang pidgin, the Chinese-English contact jargon of the treaty port (see the earlier notes on it). “Missee,” just below, is its word for a foreign lady.

ch124.anchor: the Shanghai proverb calls this breed of beggar
ch124.note: Dingba, literally a “nail-clinger”: a beggar who fastens himself to a mark and cannot be shaken off.

ch124.anchor: So the man who gave his money
ch124.note: The beggars’ cant turns the almsgiver into the “pig” (zhulou) they drive; the next sketch, “Slaughtering the Pigs,” carries the same figure over into armed robbery.

ch125.anchor: there are even those who meet a violent death
ch125.note: Sha zhulou, “slaughtering the pigs,” is the robbers’ cant for waylaying and stripping a lone traveller, the victim being the “pig”—a grimmer cousin of the beggars’ “driving the pigs” in the previous sketch.
Nianguan, the “year-gate”: the days before the New Year when debts fell due and the poor were most pressed—proverbially the hardest season to get through, and so the season of most crime.

ch126.anchor: Whenever there is one of the two affairs
ch126.note: “Red affairs” (hong shi) are weddings and other happy occasions, red being the colour of joy; “white affairs” (bai shi) are funerals, white being the colour of mourning.
Ben jie xiongdi, “brothers of this street”—the local toughs’ flattering name for themselves; the “payoff” (na kaixiao) they levy is a protection-style tax on every neighbourhood event.

ch127.note: The author glosses his own word: baixiangren, rendered throughout this translation as “hoodlum,” which he equates with liumang, a hooligan. Its literal sense, “man-about-town,” is discussed in an earlier note.
The source has fan tu, “dealing in earth”—tu, “native earth,” being the trade word for raw opium.

ch127.anchor: set about what they call the
ch127.note: Jiang jintou, Wu-dialect for bargaining over terms or a price; here it is the hoodlum’s shakedown dressed up as a “negotiation.”

ch128.note: The anmu, the theatre’s seat-agents or ushers, who steered patrons to their places, ran accounts for the regulars and lived off tips and commissions.
Jieye, “the receiving trade,” the seat-agents’ own name for their calling.

Shangguang quan, a “grace-us-with-your-presence ticket.” Sold to regular patrons at the festival season at a steep mark-up, it was in effect a compulsory gratuity; the same device is met earlier in the book.

ch128.anchor: Stripped bare, it is nothing but
ch128.note: Da choufeng, literally “to draw off the wind”: Shanghai slang for extracting a cut or a squeeze from someone.

ch129.anchor: someone to lend him a name and stand behind him
ch129.note: Gai paitou: gai is Wu for leaning or pawning against something, paitou a signboard or reputation. To “lean on a signboard” is to trade on the name of a powerful patron for protection.
Chengtou, a “prop” or backer, which the author equates with a baobiao, an armed escort or bodyguard.

Yaniao chou, “stinking of duck-piss,” is a vivid Wu idiom for being utterly disgraced and in a sorry, unsalvageable mess; it is paired here with tantai, to lose face (literally, to have one’s stage collapse).
The retort turns on chidou, which the author himself glosses as Shanghai slang for the fierce and domineering.
